      *Background:* High-dimensional omics data from complex experimental designs, particularly those with hierarchical structures such as repeated measures, require flexible statistical modeling approaches. While traditionally used packages for, e.g., RNA-seq analysis, include mechanisms for parameter shrinkage to increase statistical efficiency, they often limit modeling flexibility, including choices of distributional assumptions and random-effects structures necessary for hierarchical data. Currently, there is a lack of tools that enable empirical Bayes shrinkage mechanisms in hierarchical data models and support a general workflow across different types of omics data.
      *Results:* We present seqwrap, an R package that provides a flexible framework for iterative modeling of high-dimensional data using established R-based regression packages. Leveraging recent developments in the glmmTMB package, seqwrap can enable a two-step approach to fit negative binomial and Poisson observation-level random effect mixed-effects models with empirical Bayes shrinkage of model parameters. In simulations of RNA-seq data from a repeated-measures design, we use seqwrap to show that regularized models substantially outperformed non-informed models and mixed-effects models using transformed counts, with higher sensitivity for detecting differentially expressed genes while maintaining false discovery rates below nominal levels. Regularization also improved model convergence, producing valid estimates for >99.9% of gene targets compared to 85-90% for non-informed count-based models. In real-world data, flexibility in defining distributional assumptions enabled thorough examination of model assumptions and robust sensitivity analysis across modeling approaches.
      *Conclusions:* seqwrap enables flexible, principled workflows for analyzing high-dimensional data from complex experimental designs with hierarchical structures. By combining established modeling frameworks with empirical Bayes regularization, seqwrap provides improved statistical performance and model convergence compared to both transformation-based approaches and non-informed models while maintaining generalizability across diverse omics data types.
keywords: |
  High-dimensional data, RNA-seq, hierarchical models, shrinkage

## Background

<!-- Outline -->

High-dimensional data, such as those derived from high-throughput nucleotide sequencing platforms or mass spectrometry systems, are becoming increasingly commonplace in many research settings in medicine and biology, either as the primary outcome of investigations or as supporting evidence for other primary outcomes. To accommodate statistical analysis of such data, many specialized software packages have been developed. These packages are typically designed to handle data with specific distributional assumptions using a limited set of modelling formulations. For example, in the R ecosystem, high-dimensional gene expression data derived from microarrays is commonly analyzed using limma [@ritchie_limma_2015], which employs a Gaussian model. However, when gene expression data are derived from next-generation sequencing platforms, gene counts are analyzed using models that assume a negative binomial distribution in packages such as DESeq2 [@love_moderated_2014] and edgeR [@robinson_edger_2010]. Although limma, DESeq2, and edgeR all incorporate information from the whole data set in the estimation of differential expression through shrinkage of dispersion or location parameters [@ritchie_limma_2015; @love_moderated_2014; @robinson_edger_2010], modelling is done on a gene-by-gene basis. However, these packages are limited in their ability to analyze data from more complex study designs, including data with hierarchical structure, a model feature that is important to recover relevant effects in such data sets [@cui2016].

To address this limitation, multiple additional software packages have been developed across both R and Python ecosystems, including packages for describing higher-order network structures in such data [@chentsao2024; @langfelder2008], [and for performing variable selection among high-dimensional predictors (e.g., gene-environment interaction studies) [@fan2025; @fan2026; @chen2024].]{custom-style="edits"} However, as target-wise analysis (e.g., gene-by-gene differential expression) serves as an important step in describing, e.g., effects of experimental manipulation, packages specifically designed for repeated measures data, such as lmerseq[@vestal_lmerseq_2022], Dream [@hoffman_dream_2021], rmRNAseq [@nguyen_rmrnaseq_2020], glmmseq [@lewis_glmmseq_2022], PairedFB [@bian_pairedfb_2019], ShrinkBayes [@van_de_wiel_shrinkbayes_2014], MCMSeq [@vestal_mcmseq_2020] were developed. Notably, lmerseq uses a linear mixed-effects model framework to analyze transformed gene expression counts, assuming normally distributed errors [@vestal_lmerseq_2022], while glmmseq uses a negative binomial generalized linear mixed-effects model to directly model counts, both in hierarchical data, such as repeated-measures designs. Interestingly, both tools mentioned above were built using established modeling packages in the R ecosystem, lme4 [@bates_fitting_2015], nlme [@pinheiro2000], and glmmTMB [@brooks_glmmtmb_nodate], to iteratively model gene expression data on a gene-by-gene basis. Although pre-specified modeling decisions simplify the user experience, they may also limit necessary flexibility. Conversely, the R ecosystem offers a collection of packages for building regression models that account for hierarchical data (e.g., lme4, glmmTMB, lmerTest) [@brooks_glmmtmb_nodate; @kuznetsova_lmertest_2017; @bates_fitting_2015]. Additionally, several R packages are devoted to post-fitting diagnostics and analysis of such models (emmeans [@lenth_emmeans_2025], DHARMa [@DHARMa], marginaleffects [@arel-bundock_how_2024]). Together, these packages provide a rich functionality for flexible model building, including evaluation and diagnostics. However, there is a lack of tools to combine the use of these established packages in complex, high-dimensional data scenarios.

Here, we present seqwrap, an R package that provides a flexible, high-level wrapper for the iterative modeling of high-dimensional data using established R-based modeling frameworks. It simplifies the process of specifying, fitting, and evaluating both simple and complex models across multiple iterations. Additionally, using seqwrap and by leveraging recent developments in glmmTMB, we also show that information sharing across targets in a high-dimensional data set is possible using priors based on the distribution of parameter values from non-informed models in a two-step workflow. This enables a flexible empirical Bayes approach to modelling high-dimensional data from complex study designs. Together, this makes seqwrap a convenient tool for creating flexible, principled workflows for high-dimensional data, such as omics data.

## Implementation

### Features of the seqwrap R package

seqwrap is built entirely in R and designed to iteratively apply a user-defined regression model to each row (representing targets) of a data matrix populated with data such as those derived from quantification of genes, proteins, or other omics-type quantities (@fig-overview). Each column in the data matrix represents a sample, and the sample metadata is combined with the target-wise data to enable modelling with established R-based packages such as lme4, nlme, and glmmTMB. This approach enables the user to obtain target-specific estimates from a specified statistical model for downstream analyses, such as differential expression or gene set enrichment analyses. Compared to similar packages like glmmseq and lmerseq[@lewis_glmmseq_2022, @vestal_lmerseq_2022], seqwrap is designed to enable the user to select a suitable model function (e.g., `lmer` or `glmmTMB`) and specify options to allow for analysis using different distributional assumptions and any combination of fixed and random effects available in the modelling framework of choice. Currently, seqwrap has been tested for compatibility with several R-based regression modelling packages extending item-by-item high-dimensional data analysis to include flexible correlation structures and multiple response distributions (@tbl-packcomp). [As such, seqwrap supports the implementation of any hierarchical structure supported by these modelling algorithms in the syntax implemented by the algorithms]{custom-style="edits"}. Notably, using `glmmTMB` as the modeling function will allow for flexible specifications of random effects and response distributions. Additionally, priors can be used to estimate a (regularized) maximum a posteriori estimate (see Case Study). seqwrap also enables the definition of custom functions for post-fitting diagnostics and analysis.

| Package | Response distributions | Additional features | [Hierarchical structures supported^1^]{custom-style="edits"} |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| glmmTMB (`glmmTMB`) | Negative binomial, Gaussian, Beta, Poisson, Gamma, *t*-distribution, log-normal, Tweedie, Mixtures (e.g., zero-inflation) | Mixed-effects models, Model dispersion parameters, Use priors (maximum *a posteriori* estimates) | Nested and crossed random effects; explicit correlation structures (e.g., `ar1(time\|id)`, `ou(time\|id)`, `toep`, unstructured) |
| stats (`lm`, `glm`) | Binomial, Gaussian, Gamma, Poisson, Over-dispersed distributions |  | None (fixed effects only) |
| nlme (`lme`, `gls`) | Gaussian | Linear and non-linear mixed-effects models, Model variance, Specify correlation structures | Nested random effects only (e.g., `random = ~1\|site/id` in `lme`; no native support for crossed effects); correlation structures for repeated measures without random effects (e.g., `correlation = corAR1(form = ~time\|id)` in `gls`) |
| lme4 (`lmer`, `glmer`) | Gaussian, Binomial, Gamma, Poisson, Over-dispersed distributions | Linear mixed-effects models | Nested (e.g., `(1\|site/id)`) and crossed (e.g., `(1\|id) + (1\|batch)`) random effects; no built-in serial correlation structures |
| MASS (`glm.nb`, `lm.gls`) | Negative binomial, Gaussian |  | None; `lm.gls` allows a user-supplied correlation/weight matrix (e.g., `lm.gls(y ~ x, W = corMatrix)`) rather than an estimated structure |
| mgcv (`gamm`, `gam`, `bam`) | Gaussian, Tweedie, Negative binomial, *t*-distribution, Poisson (zero-inflated and censored) | Generalized additive models, Mixed-effects models | Nested random effects (`gamm`, e.g., `random = list(site = ~1, id = ~1)`, via an `nlme` backend); random-effect smooths that can represent crossed structures (e.g., `s(id, bs = "re") + s(batch, bs = "re")` in `gam`/`bam`); smooth non-linear time trends (e.g., `s(time, id, bs = "fs")`) |

: Packages tested for compatibility with seqwrap. See the official package documentation for details on the functions of each supported package. ^1^ For `mgcv`, support for crossed versus nested structures depends on the entry point: `gamm()` calls `nlme::lme()` internally and is therefore restricted to nested grouping factors, whereas `gam()` and `bam()` with random-effect smooth terms (`bs = "re"`) treat each grouping factor independently and can represent crossed designs. {#tbl-packcomp}

![Overview of the main functions in the `seqwrap` package. `seqwrap_compose` is used to populate a `swcontainer` object with data (*m* targets, *n* samples, and optionally *q* outcome variables), sample metadata (*n* sample and *k* covariates, including sample name), and optionally, target-wise data (targetdata, *m* data frames with *d* variables and *p* rows) in addition to the model function and its arguments. `seqwrap_compose` expects a sample name to indicate the variable name in the metadata containing sample identifications. The user may specify custom summary and evaluation functions. `seqwrap` uses the populated `swcontainer` to iterate over all m targets using the defined model. To combine results from seqwrap, `seqwrap_summarise` collects all results into two data frames suitable for downstream analysis.](img/overview.png){#fig-overview}

The package implements three core functions: `seqwrap_compose`, `seqwrap`, and `seqwrap_summarise` (@fig-overview, see below and supplementary material for code examples). `seqwrap_compose` accepts as input the required data sets (the high-dimensional data, sample metadata, and optionally, target-wise metadata), a selected modeling algorithm together with its arguments, and the name of the sample id variable (sample name). While the metadata remains the same across all iterations, `targetdata` provides an additional data set for target-specific values to each model. Such values could be fixed parameter values, such as dispersion values for negative binomial models estimated from preliminary models, or priors for regularizing parameters in models that allow for *maximum a posteriori* estimates (see below for an example). When the input data is a single data frame with each row representing a target and each column representing a sample, the target-specific outcome data will be represented by the letter `y` when specifying the model formula in the arguments (e.g., `formula = y ~ 1`). Data can also be supplied to `seqwrap_compose` as a named list of data frames. In this case, target-specific variables will be represented by their names and will be available for specifying a formula used by the modeling algorithm. [Importantly, the user must ensure that any required pre-processing steps are carried out before modelling as seqwrap does not include pre-processing functionality. Pre-processing, such as quality control, filtering, normalization or transformations, depending on the nature of the data, must therefore be done using appropriate tools such as, e.g., `edgeR` for library size calculations in an RNA-seq workflow [@robinson2010],  `minfi` for pre-processing Illumina methylation arrays [@fortin2014], or `QFeatures` [@qfeatures] for quantifying features in a proteomic workflow.]{custom-style="edits"}

The metadata should include all design variables used to define the model formula, as well as the variable containing the sample names corresponding to the data columns. `seqwrap_compose` also expects a list of arguments for the selected modeling function, including the model formula and additional arguments, such as those used to specify a distributional model in generalized linear models. Optionally, the user may specify functions for model summaries and evaluations, load these into the computing environment and reference them in `seqwrap_compose`. When the user does not provide custom summary or evaluation functions, the default summary and evaluation functions will provide tabular summaries of all parameter estimates (summary function) and, if available for the selected modeling algorithm, model assumptions checks (evaluation function). `seqwrap` will use custom or defined summary and evaluation functions to evaluate fitted model objects.

When combining all input into a `swcontainer` object, `seqwrap_compose` performs pre-model validation to detect potential issues before iterative model fitting. Once populated, the resulting `swcontainer` object can be supplied to `seqwrap` for iterative target-by-target modeling. `seqwrap` iterates over all targets (rows in data), or a user-specified subset of targets, which can be helpful when prototyping the model. While prototyping the model using a subset of targets, the user can also choose to return model objects for developing and testing summary or evaluation functions, or debugging the model. We do not recommend saving full model objects during full-scale iterative modeling of large data sets, as this can be very memory-intensive. `seqwrap` enables parallel processing via the `pbapply` package with a user-specified number of cores. Once initialized, `seqwrap` will merge data, fit the defined model and evaluate it with the summary and evaluation function. `seqwrap` provides progress tracking and an elapsed time estimate, which can be helpful when comparing modeling strategies for computational efficiency in the prototype step (see supplementary material).

After iterating over the data set, `seqwrap` displays a compact summary of any errors, warnings, and messages returned by the selected modeling algorithm, along with those returned from the default or user-specified summary and evaluation functions. All errors, warnings, and messages are stored in a tabular format in the result object (`seqwrap_results`) available for inspection. The results object also contains all model outputs created by the evaluation and summary functions. Models that fail to produce output (e.g., due to non-convergence) are removed from the model summaries. The `seqwrap_summarise` function collects all summaries into two data frames for further downstream analysis.


## Case studies

### Analysis of RNA-seq data

Pillon et al. [@pillon2022] investigated gene expression profiles in individuals with type 2 diabetes and healthy control individuals in response to a standardized exercise session. RNA was extracted from muscle biopsy samples obtained before, immediately after, and after a 3-hour recovery (two groups, three time-points). Paired-end RNA-sequencing was performed, and the data were submitted to the Gene Expression Omnibus (GSE202295). Here we have downloaded the available raw counts matrix data, which has been processed into counts from raw reads by NCBI. Raw read counts were filtered to retain target genes with at least 10 counts in 70% of samples for each group-time-point combination.

Using the data from Pillon et al. [@pillon2022], we are interested in baseline differences in gene expression profiles between individuals with type 2 diabetes and healthy controls. Additionally, we want to determine differences in responses to the exercise session. Since the data have been collected using a repeated-measures design, in which samples are obtained from the same individuals at three time points, we use a mixed-effects model to directly obtain estimates of the baseline differences and the differences between groups in changes from baseline, while controlling for correlations among samples due to the repeated design using a varying intercept per participant (random intercept). [Using a negative binomial (NB2) distribution for count data, we construct preliminary models for the conditional mean ($\mu_{gi}$) of gene *g* (*g* = 1, ..., *m*; the *m* rows of the `data` matrix in @fig-overview), where each observation (*i* = 1, ..., *n*; the *n* sample columns of `data`) is taken from a particular participant *j*[*i*] (*j* = 1, ..., *J*) at three time points (baseline, post-exercise (*t2*), and recovery (*t3*), where $\text{time}_{t2}$ and $\text{time}_{t3}$ are dummy variables relative to the baseline reference) belonging to one of two disease groups (normal glucose tolerance (*NGT*) and *diabetes* where *NGT* is the reference level). The model parameters $\beta_{0g}$ to $\beta_{5g}$ capture the intercept, the main effects of group and time, and their interactions. A gene-specific random intercept ($b_{g,j[i]}$, normally distributed with SD $\sigma_g$) accounts for participant-level correlation; because each of the *m* targets is fitted in a separate model, these participant intercepts are estimated per gene. An observation level offset $\operatorname{log}(\text{s}_i)$ accounts for differences in library size, where *s~i~* is the TMM-normalized library size [@robinson2010] divided by the median normalized library size. The NB2 distribution includes a dispersion parameter ($\theta_g$) to capture overdispersion.]{custom-style="edits"}

$$
\begin{align}
Y_{gi} &\sim \operatorname{NB2}(\mu_{gi}, \theta_g) \\
\operatorname{log}(\mu_{gi}) &= \eta_{gi} \\
\eta_{gi} &= \beta_{0g} + \beta_{1g} \text{group}_{\text{diabetes},i} + \beta_{2g} \text{time}_{t2,i} + \beta_{3g} \text{time}_{t3,i} +\\
&\quad \beta_{4g} ( \text{time}_{t2,i}\times\text{group}_{\text{diabetes},i}) + \\
&\quad \beta_{5g} ( \text{time}_{t3,i}\times\text{group}_{\text{diabetes},i}) + \\
&\quad \operatorname{log}(\text{s}_i) + b_{g,j[i]} \\
b_{g,j} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \sigma_g)
\end{align}
$$ {#eq-model-1}

Our model uses the parameterization $\text{Var}(Y_{gi}) = \mu_{gi} + \frac{\mu_{gi}^2}{\theta_{g}}$ so that $\theta_{g}$ represents the gene-specific inverse dispersion (as implemented in the glmmTMB package as `nbinom2`).

[Using the seqwrap package, we can define the code needed to run the model described in @eq-model-1 using the `seqwrap_compose` function (@lst-usage-m1). In the most basic setup, `seqwrap_compose` assembles required inputs for model fitting into a validated `swcontainer` object, which serves as the primary input to `seqwrap` for iterative model fitting. Required inputs include the model-fitting function (`modelfun`, e.g., `glmmTMB::glmmTMB`), the high-dimensional data, which in this case is a data frame with the first column holding the target names (@tbl-m1-data), the sample metadata (@tbl-m1-metadata), the name of the sample identifier variable (`samplename`), and a list of arguments to be passed to the model fitting function (`arguments`). These arguments must follow the conventions and syntax expected by the selected modeling framework. Optionally, the user can write custom summary and evaluation functions which will be used to evaluate the fitted model in each iteration. Here we add a custom evaluation function to capture the estimated dispersion parameter, which glmmTMB stores in the standard deviation report (in the `sdr` slot; see @lst-usage-m1). We construct a custom evaluation function that returns a data frame, which is subsequently combined using `seqwrap_summarise` with target identifications added per row. ]{custom-style="edits"}

```{r}
#| lst-label: lst-usage-m1
#| lst-cap: "Defining Model 1 as a seqwrap container object"
#| eval: false


custom_eval <- function(m) {
      out <- data.frame(
            dispersion = data.frame(summary(m$sdr))["betadisp",1],
            dispersion.se = data.frame(summary(m$sdr))["betadisp",2],
            log_mu = mean(predict(m, type = "link"))
            )
      return(out)
}



m1 <- seqwrap_compose(
      modelfun = glmmTMB::glmmTMB,
      data = counts, 
      metadata = metadata,
      eval_fun = custom_eval,
      arguments = list(
            formula = y ~ time * group + offset(ln_efflibsize) + (1|id),
            family = glmmTMB::nbinom2), 
      samplename = "seq_sample_id" 
  )

```


```{r}

# Display a gene count data set example
gene_example <- seqwrappaper::pillon_counts$countdata |>
    dplyr::select(geneid, GSM6107906, GSM6107907, GSM6107908) |>
    slice_sample(n = 6) |>

               col.names = c("geneid", "GSM6107906", "GSM6107907",
                             "GSM6107908", "\u22ef"))




```


```{r}

metadata_example <- seqwrappaper::pillon_counts$metadata |>
      filter(seq_sample_id %in% c("GSM6107906", "GSM6107907", "GSM6107908")) |>
```

[After defining the model as a seqwrap container, we use the `seqwrap` function to iterate over all targets in the data. When setting up a model run, we suggest prototyping the model by fitting a subset of the data and returning all models in the results object (see @lst-usage-seqwrap-m1). This will enable inspection of the model objects and correspondence to the expected output. After fitting the full data set, we can use `seqwrap_summarise` to combine the results into data frames. `seqwrap_summarise` will return a list containing output from summaries and evaluations, as well as a data frame containing any errors caught during model fitting.]{custom-style="edits"}

```{r}
#| lst-label: lst-usage-seqwrap-m1
#| lst-cap: "Iterating over the full data set and summarising the model fits. For prototyping we suggest using the `subset` and `return_models` arguments to save the full model object in the results. `detectCores` is used to find the number of available CPU cores."
#| eval: false


CORES <- parallel::detectCores()

m1_results <- seqwrap(m1, 
              # For prototyping:
              # return_models = TRUE,
              # subset = 1:10,
              cores = CORES
  )


m1_summaries <- seqwrap_summarise(m1_results)



```


#### Simulation study

To evaluate the performance of different models, we used the distribution of estimates from the preliminary model (@eq-model-1, @fig-m1-estimates) to simulate 20 data sets, each with 10000 genes. Simulated parameter values were used to construct the expected values of a negative binomial distribution. Two parameters (β~1~ and β~5~) were simulated using two sets of genes (1250 genes each) each with non-null effects. These effects were drawn from a uniform distribution with a minimum of 0.2 and a maximum of 1. For the β~1~ parameter, the effect was assigned a positive or negative sign with equal probability, while the parameter β~5~ was simulated with positive signs 75% of the time to match the characteristics of the observed data [@pillon2022]. We used the estimated mean-dispersion relationship to simulate dispersion parameter values from a normal distribution centered on the trend, with a SD equal to the residual standard error of a local polynomial regression model with equal weights given to all dispersion estimates or weights given to each observation proportional to the inverse standard error of the dispersion estimate. This created two dispersion scenarios, one with high and one with low variability among gene-specific dispersion parameters (@fig-m1-estimates).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of estimated parameter values (density curves; A) from Model 1 describing gene expression levels (counts) in gene-wise negative binomial models and parameter values used to simulate counts (bars; A). The mean-dispersion relationship was described using a local polynomial regression (LOESS) with the inverse of the estimated standard error was used to provide weights to the estimated curve (orange line; B). A subset of estimates are shown with size of points showing relative weight in the model. A smaller point has large a large standard error for the dispersion parameter, indicated with error bras. The estimated dispersion parameter is the inverse dispersion indicating higher overdispersion at lower estimates. The residual standard error from the LOESS model was used to simulate dispersion parameters (gray field in B)."
#| fig-width: 6.69
#| fig-height: 4.72
#| out-width: "170mm"
#| out-height: "120mm"
#| label: fig-m1-estimates


if (show_figures) {
  figure2 <- readRDS(here::here("analysis/figures/figure-2.RDS"))
  figure2
}


```

Simulated data sets were used to assess inferential performance of five types of models: The negative binomial model (already described in @eq-model-1), a Poisson model with observation-level random effects (OLRE) to handle overdispersion, and a Gaussian model with transformed count data as the dependent variable, as previously suggested [@vestal_lmerseq_2022]. The negative binomial and the Poisson OLRE models were further extended to include empirical Bayes parameter regularization using priors estimated from preliminary models. All models contained the same fixed-effect structure, including group, time, and their interaction, as well as a random intercept per participant (@eq-model-1).

The Poisson OLRE model includes both a gene-specific varying intercept term for each participant *j* (*b*~*g*,*j*\[*i*\]~) and an OLRE (*b*~*g*,*i*~) for each observation *i* in the data set. Poisson OLRE have previously been used to account for overdispersion in count data with favorable characteristics [@harrison2014], including RNA-seq data [@sun2017]. Similar to the negative binomial model (@eq-model-1), the Poisson model includes an offset term representing the size factor of the library size (*s~i~*; @eq-model-2). 

$$
\begin{align}
Y_{gi} &\sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda_{gi}) \\
\operatorname{log}(\lambda_{gi}) &= \eta_{gi} \\
\eta_{gi} &= \mathbf{X}_{i} \boldsymbol{\beta}_g + \operatorname{log}(\text{s}_i) + b_{g,j[i]} + b_{g,i}  \\
b_{g,j} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \sigma_{g[\text{participants}]}) \\
b_{g,i} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \sigma_{g[\text{observations}]})
\end{align}
$$ {#eq-model-2}

[For compactness, the intercept, the main effects of group and time, and their interactions written out in @eq-model-1 are collected into the design-matrix row $\mathbf{X}_{i}$ and the coefficient vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}_g$, so that $\mathbf{X}_{i}\boldsymbol{\beta}_g$ in @eq-model-2 and @eq-model-3 denotes the same linear combination of fixed effects.]{custom-style="edits"}

For a single gene target, the model can be fitted with the `glmmTMB` package using the Poisson family distribution and an observation-level indicator variable to add OLRE. Using `seqwrap`, the model can be readily applied to the whole gene count matrix. [The required changes to the model container used to fit model 1 (@lst-usage-m1) are accomplished by adding an observation-level random effect and changing the family argument (@lst-usage-m2). The observation-level factor corresponds to the sample name in the metadata, which makes it convenient to use this indicator for the additional random effect.]{custom-style="edits"} 

```{r}
#| lst-label: lst-usage-m2
#| lst-cap: "Defining Model 1 as a seqwrap container object"
#| eval: false


m2 <- seqwrap_compose(
      modelfun = glmmTMB::glmmTMB,
      data = counts, 
      metadata = metadata, 
      arguments = list(
            formula = y ~ time * group + offset(ln_efflibsize) + (1|id) + 
                  (1|seq_sample_id),
            family = stats::poisson), 
      samplename = "seq_sample_id" 
  )

```

To regularize parameter estimates in the negative binomial and Poisson OLRE models, we used estimates from the non-informed models (@eq-model-1, @eq-model-2) as priors in subsequent models. This empirical Bayes approach is analogous to borrowing information across genes and to the moderation of test statistics, as implemented in popular packages for RNA-seq analysis [@efron2010; @mccarthy2012; @love_moderated_2014; @robinson_edger_2010]. Priors for variance components (*b*~*g*,*i*~ and *b*~*g*,*j*\[*i*\]~) were defined using the Gamma distribution with means estimated from non-informed models and a fixed shape parameter of 2 to avoid too much density on 0. For fixed effects (β~*g*\[*c*\]~, where *c* = 1, ..., *C* indexes the fixed-effect parameters excluding the intercept), normal distributions centered on zero were used, with standard deviations taken from the distribution of parameter estimates in the non-informed models. Finally, for the negative binomial model, a normal prior was used for the dispersion parameter, with a mean equal to the expected value from the estimated mean-dispersion relationship (local polynomial regression) from non-informed models and a standard deviation equal to the residual standard deviation of the same model. The complete model formulation for the negative binomial model is shown in @eq-model-3.

$$
\begin{align}
Y_{gi} &\sim \operatorname{NB2}(\mu_{gi}, \theta_g) \\
\operatorname{log}(\mu_{gi}) &= \eta_{gi} \\
\eta_{gi} &= \mathbf{X}_{i} \boldsymbol{\beta}_g + \operatorname{log}(\text{s}_i) + b_{g,j[i]} \\
b_{g,j} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \sigma_g) \\
\sigma_{g} &\sim \operatorname{Gamma}(\tau_{b[0]}, 2) \\
\beta_{g[c]} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \tau_{c}) \\
\operatorname{log}(\theta_{g})&\sim \operatorname{Normal}(\hat{\theta}_{g}^{MLE}, \tau_g)
\end{align}
$$ {#eq-model-3}

Here, we used the `glmmTMB` package [@brooks2017a] to fit models that produce *maximum a posteriori* estimates after applying independent priors on selected parameters. Because our `seqwrap` package makes target-specific data available at each iteration, we can specify target-specific priors for the negative binomial model, and common priors used in the Poisson OLRE model. [To create an informed prior for the dispersion parameter in the negative binomial model, we use the dispersion estimates returned from the custom evaluation function used in the container object for model 1 (@lst-usage-m1). We want to estimate the association between the raw mean counts per target and the log-dispersion estimate, and fit a model to these data using a local polynomial regression (`loess`). The model's predictions are used to specify the dispersion parameter prior, with the &sigma; parameter defining the standard deviation (trend_model$s in lst-usage-m3). Next, we summarise the parameter-specific estimates from the firt model (Model 1), starting with the fixed effects and the random effect. In `glmmTMB` (version 1.1.14), priors are specified as data frames with columns prior, class and coef, with the prior defined using a character specifying the distribution and parameter values (e.g., `"normal(0,1)"`). We thus need to add the distributional form to each entry in the prior data frame, along with the class (either fixed, "fixef", or random, "ranef") and the term defining the coef. Finally, since we will use the predicted association between dispersion and raw counts as the prior for the dispersion parameter, we will store each resulting data frame in a list of equal length to the number of targets (@lst-usage-m3). After setting up the priors list, we need to define a second seqwrap container for the model, corresponding to model @eq-model-3 with priors built from the non-informed estimates. Using `seqwrap_compose` and the `targetdata` argument, the list containing the target-specific priors is defined. This makes the columns of the data frames in each list slot available in each iteration. We can then reference these columns in the data frame created by the priors argument (@eq-model-3).]{custom-style="edits"}

[When using the same prior for all targets, the target data can be a single data frame that is made available to seqwrap in each iteration. For model 5, the informed Poisson model, a single data frame is used to capture the estimates from the first non-informed model run.]{custom-style="edits"}

```{r}
#| lst-label: lst-usage-m3
#| lst-cap: "Setting up priors for the negative binomial model (Model 3)"
#| eval: false

# Combine dispersion estimates and raw mean counts
dispersion_dat <- data.frame(
  target = as.character(counts[, 1]),
  log_mu_raw = log(rowMeans(counts[, -1]))) |>
  inner_join(m1_summaries$evaluations)

# Fit a trend model
trend_model <- loess(dispersion ~ log_mu_raw, data = dispersion_dat)

# Predict dispersion for each gene based on log raw counts
# and combine into a prior.
dispersion_prior <- data.frame(
  gene = counts[, 1],
  pred = round(
    predict(
      trend_model,
      newdata = data.frame(
        log_mu_raw = log(rowMeans(counts[, -1])))), 3), 
  s = round(trend_model$s, 3)) |>
  mutate(prior = paste0("normal(", pred, ",", s, ")"))

# Summarise fixed-effects parameter values
estimate_distributions <- m1_summaries$summaries |>
    dplyr::select(target, term, estimate) |>
    dplyr::summarise(.by = term,
              m = mean(estimate),
              s = sd(estimate)) |>
    filter(!term %in%  c("(Intercept)", "sd__(Intercept)"))

# Extract the random effects distribution to fit a gamma distribution
random_sd_estimate <- m1_summaries$summaries |>
    dplyr::filter(term == "sd__(Intercept)") |>
    dplyr::select(target, term, estimate) |>
    pull(estimate)

mean_sd <- mean(random_sd_estimate)

# Combine fixed- and random effects into a common data frame
Priors_df <- bind_rows(
    data.frame(prior = paste0("normal(0, ",
                              round(estimate_distributions$s, 2), ")"),
               class = rep("fixef", 5),
               coef = estimate_distributions$term),
    data.frame(prior = paste0(
      "gamma(",
      round(mean_sd ,2),
      ",",
      2,
      ")"),
      class = "ranef",
      coef = "id")
  )

# Target specific priors in a list
Priors_list <- list()
for( j in 1:nrow( counts)) {
    df <- bind_rows(Priors_df,
                    data.frame(
                      prior =
                        dispersion_prior[dispersion_prior$gene ==
                                           counts[j,1],4],
                      class = "fixef_disp",
                      coef = "1"
                    )
    )
    Priors_list[[j]] <- df
}

# Defining a new seqwrap container
m3 <- seqwrap_compose(
      data =  counts,
      metadata =  metadata,
      samplename = "seq_sample_id",
      modelfun = glmmTMB::glmmTMB,
      eval_fun = custom_eval,
      targetdata =  Priors_list,
      arguments = alist(
            formula =  y ~ time * group + offset(ln_efflibsize) + (1|id),
            family = glmmTMB::nbinom2,
            priors = data.frame(
                  prior = prior,
                  class = class,
                  coef = coef) 
            )
      )

```




### Analysis of DNA methylation array data

```{r}
#| label: case-methylation-description
#| echo: false


# The GEO ID
gse_id   <- "GSE114763"
# Download directories for the methylation data
raw_dir  <- here::here("analysis/data/raw_data", gse_id)
pheno_file <- file.path(raw_dir, "pheno_raw.rds")

# Metadata
participant_data <- readRDS(pheno_file)

# Get sample metadata into text
sample_metadata <- participant_data |> 
      summarise(.by = participant, 
                weight = mean(weight), 
                height = mean(height), 
                age = mean(age)) |> 
      pivot_longer(weight:age) |> 
      summarise(.by = name, 
                m = mean(value), 
                s = sd(value)) |> 
      mutate(unit = c("kg", "cm", "years")) |> 
      mutate(stat = paste0(sprintf("%.1f", round(m, 1)), 
                           " (",

                           ") ", 
                           unit)) 

age <- filter(sample_metadata, name == "age") |> pull(stat)
height <- filter(sample_metadata, name == "height") |> pull(stat)
weight <- filter(sample_metadata, name == "weight") |> pull(stat)

```

[Seaborne et al. [@seaborne2018;@seaborne2018b] investigated whether human skeletal muscle retains an epigenetic memory of earlier hypertrophy-inducing resistance training. For this purpose, eight previously untrained male participants (mean (SD): age, `r age`; weight, `r weight`; height, `r height`) completed a sequential protocol with two seven-week periods of resistance-exercise training (RET) separated by a seven-week unloading period without RET. RET periods included two weekly sessions targeting the lower limbs and one weekly session targeting the upper body (seven and five exercises, respectively; four sets of ten repetitions per exercise). Skeletal muscle biopsies were sampled from *m. vastus lateralis* on five occasions: before the intervention, 30 min after the first exercise session, and after the completion of each of the seven-week periods. Genomic DNA was extracted from muscle biopsy samples (DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit, Qiagen, Manchester, UK) and bisulfite-converted before amplification, fragmentation, and hybridization using the Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC BeadChip protocol [@seaborne2018;@seaborne2018b].]{custom-style="edits"}


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: read-gset-from-rds

# Count the number of probes in the final data set. 
gset <- readRDS(
    here::here("analysis/data/derived_data/seaborne-gset-quantile.RDS")
  )

probes <- dim(gset)[1]


```


[We downloaded a total of 40 samples from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GSE114763). We retained 38 samples for subsequent analysis after removal of two samples identified by Seaborne et al. as unreliable in preliminary quality control analysis [@seaborne2018b]. Raw array files were further processed using the minfi package [@aryee2014]. Files were read and normalized using between-array quantile normalization (`preprocessQuantile()`), stratified by probe region and applied with outlier correction, before filtering. Probes were filtered from the data set if they (1) failed detection in any retained sample, (2) overlapped common SNPs at the target CpG or single-base extension site, (3) appeared on published lists of cross-reactive EPIC probes [@pidsley2016;@mccartney2016] (using the maxprobes package), or (4) mapped to the sex chromosomes (all male cohort). After filtering, `r probes` probes remained for analysis.]{custom-style="edits"}

[Between-array quantile normalization returns methylation as a log ratio rather than as a pair of intensities. For each sample and CpG site the M-value was therefore taken directly as $M =\log_2(\text{Meth}/\text{Unmeth})$, and the methylation ratio, also called the &beta; value, was derived from it by the inverse logit, $\beta = 2^{M}/(1 + 2^{M})$. No offset constant was used. As the &beta; values are restricted to the interval (0,1) the variance is dependent on the mean and will shrink when approaching the boundary. Although the &beta; values has a convenient interpretation as the approximate methylation percentage for a specific CpG, statistical models that assumes constant variance fail to account for the floor and ceiling effects induced by the boundaries [@du2010]. To mitigate this problem, the logit transform of &beta; values is commonly used for statistical analysis of per-site differential methylation [@du2010;@laird2010]. This metric, also called the M-value, is free of boundary effects and has been shown to have favorable statistical properties when a statistical model assuming homoscedasticity is applied as compared to the same model being used with &beta; values as the response variable [@du2010]. However, the &beta; values could more appropriately be modeled using beta regression, e.g., as implemented in the glmmTMB package [@brooks2017a].]{custom-style="edits"}

[In small samples modeled with Gaussian mixed-effects models, restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation and subsequent derivation of p-values from a corrected reference distribution, using, e.g., Satterthwaite's method to approximate the denominator degrees of freedom (DDF), will lead to acceptable type I error rates [@luke2017]. Conversely, failing to account for small sample bias will inflate the type I error rate and invalidate inference. For generalized linear mixed models, REML estimation has not been standard practice due to difficulties extending the method to non-normal outcomes [@maestrini2026]. However, several extensions have been proposed and shown to reduce small-sample bias when estimating variance components in generalized linear mixed models [@maestrini2026]. Similar to REML estimation, Satterthwaite's method for approximating DDF, which was not previously implemented in software for modeling non-normal outcome variables, is now available in the glmmTMB package. We therefore chose to evaluate the characteristics of these modeling choices using a permutation experiment to assess the type I error rate and power in the small-sample-size but large-target-size methylation data set. We also used the full data set [@seaborne2018] to show that seqwrap can handle a large number of targets (`r probes` CpG sites).]{custom-style="edits"}

#### Model building and permutation experiment

[Two target models were formulated based on the experimental design with the same linear predictor ($\eta$) for CpG site *c* (*c* = 1, ..., *m*; the *m* rows of the `data` matrix) and observation *i* (*i* = 1, ..., *n*; the *n* sample columns of `data` and the number of rows in the metadata), with each observation belonging to a participant *j*[*i*] (*j* = 1, ..., *J*, *J* = 8). In the first model (@eq-model-m), M-values were assumed to follow a normal distribution with a conditional mean ($\mu_{ci}$) for each CpG site.]{custom-style="edits"} 

$$
\begin{align}
Y_{ci} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(\mu_{ci}, \sigma_c) \\
\mu_{ci} &= \eta_{ci} \\
\eta_{ci} &= \mathbf{X}_{i} \boldsymbol{\beta}_c + b_{c,j[i]} \\
b_{c,j} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \sigma_{c[\text{participant}]}) \\
\end{align}
$$ {#eq-model-m}

[In @eq-model-m, $\mathbf{X}_{i} \boldsymbol{\beta}_c$ expands to an intercept ($\beta_{0c}$) representing the site-specific mean in the reference sampling time-point, and parameters for indicator variables representing follow-up sampling time points ($\beta_{1c}$, 30 min after the first session; $\beta_{2c}$, after the first 7-week loading period; $\beta_{3c}$, after the unloading period, and; $\beta_{4c}$, after the reloading period). A participant- and site-specific intercept ($b_{c,j}$) accounted for the correlation between samples within participants and enabled parameters to be interpreted as within-participant comparisons between the reference and follow-up sampling time-points.]{custom-style="edits"} 

[The second model uses the beta regression model proposed by @ferrari2004 as implemented in glmmTMB [@brooks2017a] (@eq-model-beta) that uses a logit link to connect the linear predictor to the conditional mean ($\mu_{ci}$, $0 < \mu < 1$) and the precision parameter ($\phi_{c}$, $\phi > 0$) that determines the variance as $\operatorname{Var}(y) = \frac{\mu(1-\mu)}{1+\phi}$ [@ferrari2004].]{custom-style="edits"} 

$$
\begin{align}
Y_{ci} &\sim \operatorname{Beta}(\mu_{ci}, \phi_c) \\
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_{ci}) &= \eta_{ci} \\
\eta_{ci} &= \mathbf{X}_{i} \boldsymbol{\beta}_c + b_{c,j[i]} \\
b_{c,j} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \sigma_{c[\text{participant}]}) \\
\end{align}
$$ {#eq-model-beta}

[As described above for the RNA-seq models, to fit the two models using the seqwrap package, we first organize the methylation data matrix so that each row represents a specific CpG site. The first column of the data frame contains CpG site names, and the following columns represent samples (`mdata` and `betadata`, respectively, @lst-usage-m67). The `metadata` is organized to include the factor variables needed to fit the model (participant and time-point identifiers) and a variable containing the sample name corresponding to the column names of the `data` data frame. REML is not the default estimator in glmmTMB, so we need to explicitly set `REML = TRUE` for fits estimated with REML. As we are interested in evaluating the use of the Satterthwaite correction for deriving p-values, we also define a custom summary function for these models (@lst-usage-m67). Using the generic summary for glmmTMB objects with `ddf = "satterthwaite"` we retrieve the p-values and approximated degrees of freedom. We combine the output so that both p-values are returned.]{custom-style="edits"} 

```{r}
#| lst-label: lst-usage-m67
#| lst-cap: "Specifying models for the DNA methylation data set using REML."
#| eval: false



# A custom summary function
custom_summary <- function(m) {
      # The same statistic read against two reference distributions.
      #  z reference
      wald <- coef(summary(m))$cond
      # t reference, Satterthwaite ddf
      # The Satterthwaite computation needs a second differentiation of the
      # likelihood and can fail on a degenerate fit where the plain Wald
      # table is still returned, so a site loses p_satt only rather than
      # dropping out entirely.
      satt <- tryCatch(coef(summary(m, ddf = "satterthwaite"))$cond,
                       error = function(e) NULL)
      i <- if (is.null(satt)) NA_integer_ else match(rownames(wald),
                                                    rownames(satt))

    data.frame(
      term      = rownames(wald),
      estimate  = wald[, "Estimate"],
      std.error = wald[, "Std. Error"],
      p_wald    = wald[, "Pr(>|z|)"],
      ddf       = if (is.null(satt)) NA_real_ else satt[i, "ddf"],
      p_satt    = if (is.null(satt)) NA_real_ else satt[i, "Pr(>|t|)"],
      row.names = NULL
    )
  }


# Preparing the swcontainer objects for REML M and beta models
m_model <- seqwrap_compose(
  modelfun = glmmTMB::glmmTMB,
  data = mdata,
  metadata = metadata,
  summary_fun = custom_summary,
  samplename = "geo_accession",
  arguments = list(
    formula = y ~ time + (1 | participant), 
    REML = TRUE
  )
)

beta_model <- seqwrap_compose(
  modelfun = glmmTMB::glmmTMB,
  data = betadata,
  metadata = metadata,
  summary_fun = custom_summary,
  samplename = "geo_accession",
  arguments = list(
    formula = y ~ time + (1 | participant),
    family = glmmTMB::beta_family(), 
    REML = TRUE
  )
)

```

[Note that the when the family argument is empty in glmmTMB, the Gaussian (normal) distribution is assumed.]{custom-style="edits"} 

[To evaluate the characteristics of the two models we performed a permutation experiment on a subset (n = 1000) of CpG sites representing different strata of average &beta; values. Over 200 iterations, systematic time-effects were removed by resampling the time variable within participants creating plasmode [@gadbury2008] data sets with a permuted time variable. This retained the within-participant correlation between samples while removing the association between time and methylation status. The permutation was used to create a null-distribution enabling the estimation of the type 1 error rate of each model. In 20% of the subset, balanced per strata, effects were added to the permuted data set on a specific time-point to enable estimation of the statistical power of model. Effects were added on the M value scale (0.1, 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8 balanced between positive and negative signs) from which data were transformed to the &beta; scale ($\beta = \frac{2^M}{1+2^M}$, since $M = \operatorname{log}_2(\frac{\beta}{1-\beta})$ [@du2010;@laird2010;@fortin2014]). Our approach deviates from the workflow for the creation plasmode data sets suggested by @gadbury2008 but enables systematic evaluation of model characteristics at tracable magnitudes and direction of effects between data sets (M and &beta; values, respectively). After each iteration, type I error rates where estimated as the proportion of p-values < 0.05 among true null sites. Power was estimated among sites with added effects as the percentage of sites with p-values below the empirical critical value.]{custom-style="edits"} 

[Following the permutation experiment, we fitted the models using the full data sets of &beta;, and M-values and estimated the site-specific effect as contrasts between the baseline and follow-up time-points.]{custom-style="edits"}

## Results

### RNA-seq simulation study

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false


true_effects <- readRDS(here::here("analysis/data/derived_data/true_effects.RDS"))


gene.counts <- true_effects |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = effect, values_from = n) |> 
  mutate(total = true.negative + true.positive) |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = true.negative:total) |> 
  summarise(.by =c(name),
            m = round(mean(value),0), 
            s = sd(value), 
            min = round(min(value),0), 
            max = round(max(value),0))



```

Before assessing the performance of the different modelling approaches, the simulated data sets were filtered for low-count targets. On average, `r gene.counts[3,2]` genes were retained after filtering of low-count targets, of which `r gene.counts[2,2]` (min-max, `r gene.counts[2,4]`-`r gene.counts[2,5]`) were true positives and `r gene.counts[1,2]` (`r gene.counts[1,4]`-`r gene.counts[1,5]`) were true negatives for each parameter of interest (baseline group differences, β~1~, and the second group-time interaction parameter, β~5~). Variability in the simulated gene dispersion parameter and sample size affected the number of retained targets, with more targets retained at lower dispersion variability and with larger sample sizes (Supplementary Figure 4).

```{r}
#| echo: false

convergence_stats <- readRDS(here::here("analysis/data/derived_data/convergence_stats.RDS"))

conv_stats <- convergence_stats |> 
  mutate(conv = 100 * ( conv / ntotal ), 
         conv.nonstrict = 100 * (conv.nonstrict / ntotal) ) |> 
  summarise(.by = c(model, disp_scenario), 
            m.conv = mean(conv), 
            m.conv.ns = mean(conv.nonstrict), 
            s.conv = sd(conv), 
            s.conv.ns = sd(conv.nonstrict)) 


```

Next, using seqwrap, we fitted the filtered simulated data sets to the different models. We were unable to retrieve model estimates from some simulated gene targets due to failed model convergence or singular fits. Most notably, using the strict criteria of filtering out singular fits from the results [@vestal_lmerseq_2022], on average `r round(conv_stats[3,3],1)`%, (SD among data sets: `r round(conv_stats[3,5],1)`) of potential targets were returned from the Gaussian model of transformed counts under the high variability dispersion scenario. The non-informed negative binomial model also had considerable loss of gene estimates (`r round(conv_stats[1,3],1)`% (`r round(conv_stats[1,5],1)`) targets with estimates). In contrast, the non-informed Poisson OLRE model performed slightly better (`r round(conv_stats[4,3],1)`% (`r round(conv_stats[4,5],1)`)). Under the low-variability dispersion scenario, all three models performed better by producing estimates in `r round(conv_stats[6,3],1)`% (`r round(conv_stats[6,5],1)`), `r round(conv_stats[8,3],1)`% (`r round(conv_stats[8,5],1)`), and `r round(conv_stats[9,3],1)`% (`r round(conv_stats[9,5],1)`) of all potential models. Interestingly, the regularized alternatives to the negative binomial and the Poisson OLRE models produced estimates for practically all potential gene targets (\>99.9%). Relaxing the criteria for the Gaussian model also yielded estimates for almost all potential gene targets (\>99.9%; supplementary Figure 5).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Data processing in figure 3
source(here::here("analysis/figures/figure-3.R"))


avg_sensitivity <- est |>
  filter(true_effect == "pos") |>


  summarise(.by = c(term, model, dataset, size, disp_scenario),
            true_positive = sum(true_positive,
                                na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  inner_join(true_effects |>
               filter(effect == "true.positive")) |>

  mutate(sensitivity = 100 * (true_positive / n)) |> 
  
  summarise(.by = c(term, model, size, disp_scenario), 
            sensitivity = mean(sensitivity)) |> 
  filter(size == "medium") 
  
  

```

When comparing models for their sensitivity, i.e., the capability to identify targets as differentially expressed (using FDR-adjusted p-values \< 0.05) among simulated genes with non-null population effects, the regularized negative binomial model, on average, outperformed all other models across dispersion scenarios and sample sizes, except in small data sets in the low-variability scenario (@fig-figure2 A). Notably, the Gaussian model of transformed counts performed considerably worse, with sensitivities approximately equal to those of the regularized negative binomial model with half the sample size (@fig-figure2 A). Comparing the negative binomial models to the Poisson OLRE models, only minor differences were detected.

Coincidentally, in most cases, regularizing the negative binomial and Poisson OLRE models improved the correlation between the ranked estimated effects and the ranked population effects used to simulate the data for truly differentially expressed targets (@fig-figure2 B; Supplementary Figure 7). The regularized versions of the count-based models also performed better than the model for transformed counts (@fig-figure2 B). Together, these results indicate that regularized count-based models are better at recovering population gene expression patterns.

After p-value adjustment, the negative binomial and Poisson OLRE models had slightly higher false discovery rates for the interaction-effect (β~5~) parameter estimates under the low-variability scenario compared to the Gaussian-transformed counts model, a difference that was rescued by regularization. The interaction effect yielded more false discoveries under the high-variability scenario, with the largest sample sizes producing the most. An analysis of the raw p-value distributions indicated that, particularly for the interaction effect, the distributions were non-uniform in most models and simulation scenarios, suggesting that the models were unable to account for the variation in the data (Supplementary Figure 6). However, all models displayed false discoveries at rates lower than the nominal 5% level (@fig-figure2 C).

Collectively, the results from our simulation study support the use of the regularized negative binomial or Poisson OLRE models for inference in our real-world data set. These models are more sensitive in detecting truly differentially expressed gene targets. They also more accurately recover population gene rankings while minimizing false discoveries. These models are also less prone to failing to converge, thereby maximizing the available information from the dataset.

```{r}
   # For model m3, is singular is the main culprit

      filter(isSingular == "TRUE") |> 
      summarise(.by = model,

      summaries$m1_results$evaluations |> 
      mutate(model = "m1"),
      summaries$m2_results$evaluations |> 
            mutate(model = "m2"),

      summaries$m4_results$evaluations |> 
            mutate(model = "m4"),
      summaries$m5_results$evaluations |> 
            mutate(model = "m5")) |> 
      filter(convergence == 0 | pdHess == TRUE) |> 
      group_by(model) |>

   # For model m3, is singular is the main culprit

     group_by(model) |>

stat <- bind_rows(
      summaries$m1_results$summaries|>
    mutate(model = "m1"), 
      summaries$m2_results$summaries|>
    mutate(model = "m2"), 
      summaries$m3_results$summaries|>
    mutate(model = "m3"), 
      summaries$m4_results$summaries|>
    mutate(model = "m4"), 
      summaries$m5_results$summaries|>
    mutate(model = "m5")  ) |> 

  # This filter away singular fits from m3
  inner_join(targets_models) |>

  filter(term %in% c("groupT2D", "timepost:groupT2D", "timerec:groupT2D")) |>

  # Adjust p-values and calculate MSD
  mutate(.by = c(model, term), fdr = p.adjust(p.value, method = "fdr")) |>
  # Approximate CI
  mutate(
    lwr = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * std.error,
    upr = estimate + qnorm(0.972) * std.error,
    msd = if_else(estimate > 0, lwr, -upr)
  )
      

# Baseline differences

  filter(term == "groupT2D", 
         fdr < 0.05) 
  
sig_gene_baseline <- paste0(sig_gene_baseline[1,1][[1]],", fold-change: ",
       round(mean(sig_gene_baseline$estimate),2),
       " (T2D vs. control), FDR < ", 
       round(max(sig_gene_baseline[1,12]),3))
```

### RNA-seq real-world data analysis

Similarly to the simulation study results, modelling the real-world data also led to a larger number of models that did not reach convergence or the criteria of non-singular fits in the Gaussian model of transformed counts (`r m3_nonest`%). Among the count-based models, the non-informed negative binomial model had `r m1_nonest`% gene targets without valid estimates. Regularized models returned estimates for practically all gene targets (@fig-figure3 A).

We compared models for their expected out-of-sample performance using AIC, restricting the comparison to models with the same regularization structure. We found that the regularized Poisson OLRE model performed better than the negative binomial model in most cases (\>80%). Both non-informed models were comparable (@fig-figure3 B).

At baseline, only one target was declared as differentially expressed in the non-informed models (`r sig_gene_baseline`). However, as expected, dramatic differences in gene expression changes in response to exercise (3-hour recovery time-point) were observed between disease groups, with the most sensitive model, the regularized Poisson OLRE, identifying 2877 gene targets as differentially expressed (FDR \< 0.05; @fig-figure3 C). Most gene targets declared as differentially expressed between groups at the recovery time-point were common in all count-based models (30%; @fig-figure3 C). An additional 22% of the differentially expressed targets were common between the regularized models that identified considerably more targets than the non-informed models. Among the regularized models, the Poisson OLRE model and negative binomial models uniquely identified 21% and 14%, respectively. The Gaussian model of transformed counts only identified 32 gene targets as differentially expressed, all of which were also identified by the other models (@fig-figure3 C).

When we ranked genes based on their fold changes between disease groups (time × group interaction effect) and performed gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA; [@xu2024]), there were only minor differences between models in gene set rankings with the highest effect sizes (@fig-figure3, see also Supplementary Table 5), indicating that the ranked fold-changes of gene sets were similar between models. @fig-figure3 C illustrates two gene sets found to be enriched among the top positively and negatively ranked genes in the T2D vs. control comparison (time × group interaction).

### DNA methylation analysis

```{r}
#| label: get-permute-data
#| echo: false


# list files in permutation results folder
# Versioned to match the script: permutation/ holds the earlier two-arm run
# (beta, m) with the old evaluation column names, permutation_v2/ the
# four-arm run (beta, beta_reml, m, m_reml_satt).
out_dir <- here::here("analysis/data/derived_data/permutation_v4")
perm_files <- list.files(
  out_dir,
  pattern = "^perm_\\d+\\.RDS$",
  full.names = TRUE
)

if (length(perm_files) == 0)
  source(
    here::here("analysis/R/methylation-error-permutation.R")
  )

n_perm <- length(perm_files)


### Reading the results back
spike_time <- "3_loading"

perm_files <- list.files(
  out_dir,
  pattern = "^perm_\\d+\\.RDS$",
  full.names = TRUE
)
perm <- lapply(perm_files, readRDS)

perm_summaries <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(perm, `[[`, "summaries"))
perm_designs <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(perm, `[[`, "design"))
perm_evals <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(perm, `[[`, "evaluations"))


# Which coefficients with the simulated effect.
#
# The added effect shifts only the samples labelled `spike_time` under the
# permuted labels. `spike_time` is set to 3_loading and
# 1_baseline is the reference level.

# alt_terms also accepts and omnibus test (not used here)
# Instead, the omnibus test is saved per target in the eval slot.
alt_terms <- c(paste0("time_permute", spike_time))

# Attach the per-iteration effects (delta, sign, stratum) to every test.
# is_alt is ground truth for a (site, term) pair, not for a site.
perm_dat <- perm_summaries |>
  dplyr::inner_join(perm_designs, by = c("iter", "target" = "id")) |>
  # Carry the per-fit convergence code across from the evaluation slot so
  # that failed fits can be dropped from the Wald error rates too. This
  # matters because the arms can fail at different rates, which would
  # quietly change which sites each arm is scored on.
  dplyr::inner_join(
    perm_evals |>
      dplyr::select(iter, target, model, convergence),
    by = c("iter", "target", "model")
  ) |>
  # delta is signed, so the test must be != 0 -- `delta > 0` would classify
  # every downward-spiked site as a null and contaminate the reference.
  dplyr::mutate(is_alt = delta != 0 & term %in% alt_terms)

stopifnot(any(perm_dat$is_alt))


# This figure extracts the &beta; values and shows the strata
# used in  the permutation study.

# Extracting full fit data     ################################################

# The results directory is VERSIONED in the same way as the permutation
# directory: full_v2/ holds the four-arm run (beta, beta_reml, m, m_reml)
# with `p_wald` and `p_satt` per contrast, the latter on the REML arms only.
# The earlier two-arm files in the derived_data root (beta-model-full.RDS,
# m-model-full.RDS) carry a different summary schema and are superseded by it.
full_dir <- here::here("analysis/data/derived_data/full_v3")
full_arms <- c("beta_reml", "m_reml")
full_files <- file.path(full_dir, sprintf("%s.RDS", full_arms))

# Unlike the permutation study, a missing file is NOT refitted on the fly: the
# four arms together are close to a day of wall-clock time (see the timings
# reported below), so what is missing is reported instead.
if (!all(file.exists(full_files)))
  stop(
    "missing arm files in full_v2/: ",
    paste(basename(full_files[!file.exists(full_files)]), collapse = ", "),
    ". Run analysis/R/methylation-case-full.R first.",
    call. = FALSE
  )

# Optionally trim the read to a subset of fixed effects. All terms are kept by
# default; the four time contrasts plus the intercept over 770 441 sites is
# ~3.9 million rows per arm, so setting this to the contrast(s) actually
# reported is the lever if the render is memory-bound.
full_keep_terms <- NULL

# One arm at a time. Each arm object is on the order of 10^2 MB, so the
# per-fit diagnostics are joined on WITHIN the arm and the arm is dropped
# before the next one is read, rather than binding four whole arms and joining
# afterwards.
read_full_arm <- function(file) {
  arm <- readRDS(file)

  summaries <- if (is.null(full_keep_terms)) arm$summaries else
    dplyr::filter(arm$summaries, term %in% full_keep_terms)

  # Carry convergence, singularity and the participant SD across from the
  # evaluation slot, exactly as perm_dat does above: the arms fail at
  # different rates, so a failed fit has to be droppable from the tests
  # rather than quietly changing which sites each arm is scored on.
  dat <- summaries |>
    dplyr::inner_join(
      dplyr::select(arm$evaluations, target, convergence, singular, re_sd),
      by = "target"
    ) |>
    # Constant within an arm, so stored as factors: at this number of
    # rows the same three labels as character vectors are hundreds of
    # MB of pointers for no extra information.
    dplyr::mutate(
      model = factor(arm$model, levels = full_arms),
      estimator = factor(
        if (isTRUE(arm$meta$reml)) "REML" else "ML",
        levels = c("ML", "REML")
      ),
      scale = factor(arm$meta$scale, levels = c("beta", "M"))
    )

  # seqwrap_summarise() drops failed targets rather than returning empty
  # rows, so a target present in one slot and not the other would silently
  # shrink the arm here.
  stopifnot(nrow(dat) == nrow(summaries))

  evaluations <- dplyr::mutate(
    arm$evaluations,
    model = factor(arm$model, levels = full_arms)
  )

  # `class` and `message` come back as character vectors named by target;
  # the names are dropped so the bound frame does not carry four sets of
  # them.
  errors <- if (NROW(arm$errors)) {
    arm$errors |>
      dplyr::mutate(
        class = unname(class),
        message = unname(message),
        model = factor(arm$model, levels = full_arms)
      )
  } else NULL

  out <- list(
    dat = dat,
    evaluations = evaluations,
    errors = errors,
    meta = arm$meta
  )

  rm(arm, summaries)
  gc()

  out
}

full_list <- lapply(full_files, read_full_arm)

# full_dat:    one row per (model, site, fixed effect) -- the frame the
#              per-position analysis is read from.
# full_evals:  one row per (model, site) -- fit-level diagnostics.
# full_errors: one row per condition raised (warnings and errors), by stage.
# full_meta:   one row per arm -- what was fitted, on how many cores, how long.
full_dat <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(full_list, `[[`, "dat"))
full_evals <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(full_list, `[[`, "evaluations"))
full_errors <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(full_list, `[[`, "errors"))
full_meta <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(full_list, `[[`, "meta"))

rm(full_list)
gc(verbose = FALSE)

# `reml` in the evaluation slot is read off the fit object, not off the arm
# name (see eval_fun in the script), so this is the check that the arm
# labelling agrees with what was actually estimated. The arms are also all
# fitted on the same set of sites, which is what makes them comparable
# site-by-site.
stopifnot(
  setequal(as.character(full_evals$model), full_arms),
  all(full_evals$reml == grepl("_reml$", as.character(full_evals$model))),
  length(unique(full_meta$k)) == 1L,
  length(unique(full_meta$n)) == 1L
)

# The number of sites and samples the full run was fitted on.
n_full_sites <- unique(full_meta$k)
n_full_samples <- unique(full_meta$n)

# The contrasts: 1_baseline is the reference level, so the time terms are the
# differences from baseline. The intercept is present in full_dat but is not a
# contrast and is excluded here.
full_terms <- setdiff(unique(full_dat$term), "(Intercept)")


# Combine the full results for the target models
res <- full_dat |>
  filter(estimator == "REML") |>
  filter(term %in% c("time3_loading", "time4_unloading", "time5_reloading")) |>
  mutate(est_M = if_else(grepl("beta", model), estimate / log(2), estimate))



# Reloading gset to make code chunk independent of above
gset <- readRDS(
  here::here("analysis/data/derived_data/seaborne-gset-quantile.RDS")
)

n_fits <- dim(gset)

# Number of issues 
n_fit_issues <- full_errors |> 
      filter(stage == "fit") |> 
      summarise(.by = c(type, model), 
                n = n()) |>  
      pull(n)
      





```

For both the &beta; and M value models, REML estimation followed by the Satterthwaite correction reduced the type I error rate towards the nominal 5% level, although in the most extreme &beta; value strata the type I errors were slightly elevated (@fig-figure5 B). As the mean estimates are the same across estimators and model definitions, the standard errors were the primary source of variation in type I error rates, with smaller values in the ML model compared to the REML model fits (@fig-figure5 B).
